_: AD-24. Swechha Farm — /farm. THE PAGE D-07.13 PROMISED AND NOBODY BUILT. That ruling reopened homepage band 8 on 21 August and required it to carry two stories 'both detailed further on the inner page'; the band shipped with its hook and its button, and the button has pointed at href="#" ever since. This file is the inner page. THE TWO STORIES ARE THE SPINE AND THE ORDER: the transformation first (barren ground into a Food Forest — the client's own proper noun, capitalised), then the place you can come to (overnight school camps and day visits for students AND EDUCATORS, team meetings and retreats). Neither is a section among several. RULINGS APPLIED: F-1 this page is the PLACE and /work/projects/farm-school stays the PROGRAMME; F-2 the page ends in a phone number, not a form; F-3 school camps ship with their hole named, not filled; F-4 the stay frames come from the owner's own Airbnb listings; F-5 the farm is at Ladpuri. D-07.3 governs the two readouts and is not re-litigated here. TWO FIGURES ARE NOT IN THIS FILE ON PURPOSE — the composted leaves and the honey are the Farm School page's figures, and the build resolves them out of data/work/projects/farm-school.json so that /farm structurally cannot disagree with the page they came from. That is the /impact architecture, applied to two figures instead of thirty-two, and it is here because F-1 splits one place across two pages and a split is exactly where numbers drift.

frame.alt: Thatched mud houses on a rise above the planted rows, a track running up to them
frame._: Chosen because it is the only frame in the library that carries both stories at once: a working field in the foreground and somewhere to sleep at the top of the track. The homepage band's own hero (farm-plot-children-facilitator) is deliberately not reused — the door and the room should not be the same picture.

masthead.lead: Five acres of barren ground at Ladpuri, in the Aravallis, ninety minutes from Delhi. It is now a Food Forest and a working farm, and it is a place you can come to — for a day, for a night, or for a season.

before.head:
The ground
came first
before.lead: There is no clever way to say what this place was. It was bare. The transformation is the whole of the first story, and it is the reason nothing else on this page is a claim about intentions.

frame.alt: Bare ground and low scrub at the edge of the farm, hills on the horizon

rows.p: Not degraded, not marginal — bare. The soil had no organic matter worth the name and nothing on it held water for longer than it took to run off.

rows.h: Then trees, and then everything that follows trees
rows.p: Most of them native, because a native tree is the one the birds and the insects here already know what to do with. Shade came, then leaf litter, then soil, then the things that live in soil.

rows.h: It is a story of transformation, and it is not finished
rows.p: A food forest is not a planting, it is a succession. The canopy that is going in now is for a farm nobody working here today will see at its best.

forest.head:
What grows
there now
forest.lead: The inventory is the evidence. A barren field does not have a manifest, and everything in this one had to be put there and kept alive.

figures.label: Trees, most of them native
figures.period: as counted by the Executive Director, August 2026

figures.label: Saplings in the native nursery
figures.period: standing stock, no start year sourced

resolved.label: Dead leaves composted into soil on site

systems.p: Layered rather than planted in rows — canopy, understorey, ground. It is the part of the farm that is deliberately least like a field.
Grown to be eaten, including by the people staying here. What the kitchen serves is mostly what the beds produced that week.
Twenty cows. The milk, the butter and the ghee on the table are theirs, and the dung is where the compost cycle starts.
Small, and kept as part of the cycle rather than as a unit of production.
Twenty thousand saplings. It is what makes the tree count go up, and it is why plantings elsewhere can be native without a supply problem.
The farm's own waste stream, closed on the farm. Leaves and dung in at one end, soil out at the other.
Hives that have to be worked, not watched. They teach more about what a monoculture costs than any lesson does, without anybody saying the word.
Planted for the insects rather than for the look of it, which is why it is at its best when it looks untidy.
Fodder, grown without soil, to carry the herd through the months when nothing green will grow outside.

systems.h: Mud houses, and other permaculture prototypes
systems.p: Built to be lived in and then watched. A prototype that nobody sleeps in has not been tested.

works.head:
How the place
keeps itself
works.lead: None of this is a demonstration model. If a system stops producing, it stops teaching, and it gets fixed rather than relabelled.

frame.alt: Four people working along freshly drawn furrows, sowing by hand

rows.h: Water is caught where it falls
rows.p: Swales, bundhs and ponds, so that rain slows down and goes into the ground instead of off it. The farm's own supply is groundwater, and the works are what put it back.

rows.h: Waste is a raw material or it is a failure
rows.p: Leaves and dung go into the vermicompost lab and come out as the soil the beds are planted in. Nothing is carted off the farm to become somebody else's problem.

rows.h: Solar, and an honest amount of it
rows.p: Enough to matter, not enough to pretend the grid is not there. When the power goes, an inverter carries it — and out here the power goes.

come.head:
Ways to
come
come.lead: The second story is the simpler one: this is a place you can turn up at. Four doors, and they are genuinely different lengths of stay rather than the same visit priced three ways.

doors.name: A day visit
doors.p: A bus and a packed lunch. One thing done with your hands, and back the same day. It is the widest door and the one most people come through — and it is open to educators on their own account, not only to schools bringing a group.
doors.who: Schools, colleges, families, individuals — and teachers and facilitators, who are named in the brief as their own audience.

frame.alt: A facilitator and children standing around a farm plot

doors.name: School camps, overnight
doors.p: A night on the farm changes what a day out can be: the animals get fed twice, the dark is genuinely dark, and the morning belongs to whoever is up for it.

frame.alt: The mud houses lit from inside after dark, their windows warm against the field

doors.name: Team meetings and retreats
doors.p: There is a table under thatch with the field on three sides of it. The farm does not distinguish much between a school group and a board, and neither do the chores.
doors.who: Organisations, teams and boards wanting the city to stop being the reference point for two days.

frame.alt: An open pavilion under thatch, drapes tied back around a round table and chairs

doors.name: Stays and internships
doors.p: Weeks rather than hours. An internship is meant to end with a person running part of this place unsupervised; if it ends in a certificate, it was a longer day visit. Shorter stays are simply that — you sleep in a mud house and lend a hand with whatever the day is doing.
doors.who: Interns and researchers from India and abroad, and anyone who wants to stay.

frame.alt: Inside an A-frame mud house — a bed under the bamboo apex, a small window at the far end

conditions.head:
It is not
a hotel
conditions.lead: This is the part most places leave out, so it goes near the top rather than in a footnote. Everything here is true of the farm on a good day.

frame.alt: A washroom built into a mud wall, a basin and dried grass in the alcove

rows.p: This is agricultural land. There is an inverter, so you will not be left in the dark, but you will notice.

rows.h: There is no wi-fi, and no television
rows.p: Mobile data works. That is the whole provision, and for a good number of people it is the reason to come.
Drawn here and filtered for drinking. It is not bottled and it does not taste like a city's.

rows.h: The nearest shop is a couple of kilometres away
rows.p: Bring what you cannot do without. There is a working kitchen if you would rather cook, and food from the farm if you would not.

rows.h: The food is what the farm grew
rows.p: Cooked with what is local and mostly what is ours, which means the menu is the season rather than a list.
Cows, bees, birds, buffalo, goats and chickens, none of them arranged for visitors. Dogs are welcome to come with you.

conditions.quote: It's not a hotel, it's natural, it's rustic. It's a real farm.
conditions.quote_attr: Vimlendu Jha, on the farm's own listing

waiting.head:
What we cannot
tell you yet
waiting.lead: Two things a reader has every right to ask, which this page cannot answer today. They are named here rather than papered over, and each one is a single fact away from being answerable.

claims.what: How many students can sleep over, in what, and with how many adults. Overnight school camps are real and they run, but no capacity, no sleeping arrangement and no supervision ratio is written down anywhere we can cite.
claims.unlocks: One line — beds, buildings, ratio — and the school camp door stops being a description and becomes something a teacher can plan a term around.

claims.what: How many people have been through this farm. Every other item on the work register counts its participants. This one counts its compost.
claims.unlocks: One participation figure with a period, and the farm can be read alongside the rest of the work instead of beside it.

sheet.head:
The nursery,
the hives,
the herd
sheet.lead: Three of the systems, photographed here. They are the ones that produce something a visitor can hold, taste or carry away, which is why they are the ones a day visit almost always ends at.

frames.alt: Cows on open ground at sunrise in warm haze
A honeybee feeding on a mustard flower in full bloom
Young plants at knee height in a nursery bed

sheet.note: No frame here carries a date, because no date on this page is sourced. What each one shows is what it says it shows.

act.head: Come and see
act.lead: There is no booking form, and that is deliberate — every way of coming here is different enough that it starts with a conversation. Say which of the four doors you mean and roughly when.
act.email_note: For school camps, courses and retreats, which are arranged rather than booked.

onward.p: The programme that runs here — the five C's, the courses, and what a stay is actually for.
The farm is one of the things Swechha does. The register is the rest of them.
